newsitem.title: GERMANY: Aluminium prices seen weak in near term.
newsitem.headline: Aluminium prices seen weak in near term.

text.p: LME broker Rudolf Wolff & Co Ltd sees aluminium prices vulnerable in the near term, but steadier in 1997 and 1998, Wolff sources said in an interview.

"The market at the moment is somewhat depressed...the next month or two, we're likely to see lower prices but I don't wish to get overly bearish about that," Wolff's marketing manager and senior account executive Brian Woodbridge said during the Metal Bulletin aluminium conference here..
"Lower prices quite often pull out consumers who are waiting in the wings for that price."
In theory, the current contango supported projections for average prices of around $1,520-1,530 a tonne in 1997 and $1,620-1,630 in 1998, against current levels around $1,470.
"If we had a balance around $1,600 everbody would be happy, consumers would not be paying too much and producers would be making good money," Woodbridge said.
"I therefore don't think we will have a sustained period of very low levels of $1,400 or below. We may visit that price level but I don't think fundamentals are that bad.
"We are in the doldrums but there is a balanced supply situation and there won't be any great increase in production coming on line in the next year.
"The odd expansion, which might be put into practice, will take at least one or two years to be on line.
"North American demand is looking reasonable, the Far East is ticking over -- it's only Europe that is lagging behind."
Simon Thompson, managing director of Wolff's Hamburg, Warsaw and Budapest operations, said the picture in Europe was mixed, with automotive products doing very well.
"Quite a lot of people at this conference are trying to be bullish...in some areas in the Far East people are telling me they can't get the aluminium quick enough," he said.
"Producers there complain premiums are not high enough.
"I would go along with the chance of short- to medium-term price weakness, with the medium to longer term much better.
"But the German consumers are noticeably absent here, and that is perhaps disappointing."
In the longer term, Woodbridge saw vast demand potential in emerging markets such as India and China -- "not overnight, but this can be put into the equation."
He also questioned the level of Commonwealth of Independent States exports in 1997, supporting analysts' views that this factor should underpin prices.
"It's a balancing act in the CIS...there are always problems -- supply, cash flows...," he said.
"I don't think you will have a smooth transition to increased volumes or better quality material."
But the Wolff executives saw the upside for prices limited in 1997 because demand was unlikely to move sharply higher and idle capacity might be activated fast.
"Some producers are able to make money even at $1,500, not $1,800 as was said a few months ago. Who knows what they will do," Woodbridge said.
He added that aluminium had been hit by weakness in copper following the Sumitomo affair.
Thompson said unofficial discussions at the 600-strong conference focused on physical non-European producer/trader business.
